screens.title: Advanced Monitoring and Troubleshooting CI/CD Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to make CI/CD pipelines reliable by adding deep observability, event-driven automation, and audit trails. We start with CloudWatch logs and metrics so you can see what's happening in builds, tests, and deployments. Then we use EventBridge to react to failures automatically, and CloudTrail to trace who or what changed permissions or resources. You will also learn systematic troubleshooting steps: reproduce failures locally, isolate the failing action, use verbose logging and the IAM policy simulator, and use AWS CLI methods to inspect executions. Finally, we cover notification design and escalation so incidents reach the right people quickly. These practices reduce mean time to detection and recovery, and help prevent recurring outages. For example, you will configure an alarm on PipelineExecutionFailed and an EventBridge rule that sends an SNS notice, then test by intentionally breaking a deployment. That hands-on workflow ties monitoring, automation, and auditing into a repeatable operational pattern.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Advanced Monitoring
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Advanced Monitoring and Troubleshooting CI/CD Pipelines

Deepen pipeline observability with CloudWatch logs, metrics, and alarms. Automate responses using EventBridge and use CloudTrail for secure auditing. These practices shorten incident time and prevent repeat failures.

In this lesson
CloudWatch
Logs, metrics, alarms and dashboards for pipeline health.
EventBridge
Route pipeline events to Lambda, SNS, or SQS for automation.
CloudTrail
Audit who changed IAM or pipeline resources.
Coming up

Hands-on alarm and rule creation, a sample failure test, and practical troubleshooting checklists you can apply immediately to production pipelines.

Pipeline observability map
Visual overview
Logs
Build and agent logs streamed to CloudWatch Logs; use Logs Insights to query.
Metrics
Standard pipeline and build metrics feed dashboards and alarms.
Events
EventBridge rules trigger automation when stages or actions fail.
Audit
CloudTrail records API calls for security and post-incident forensics.
Quick start
Create an alarm on PipelineExecutionFailed, then add an EventBridge rule to publish to an SNS topic. Test by creating a controlled failure and inspect CloudTrail for any recent IAM changes.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

Learn, understand, and apply monitoring, event rules, auditing, and troubleshooting for CI/CD pipelines.

01
Implement CloudWatch monitoring
Configure logs, metrics, and dashboards for CodePipeline, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy. This matters because real-time visibility makes failures actionable.
Mnemonic: Metrics + Logs = Insight
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Configure EventBridge rules

Mnemonic: Event → Rule → Action
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Use CloudTrail for auditing

Mnemonic: Who, When, What

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Notifications & Reliability
screens.narratorSegment: This second objective screen focuses on notifications, escalation policies, and testable practices. You will learn to design granular notification topics for different event types so messages reach the correct teams. For example, separate SNS topics for critical production failures and for development pipeline noise prevent alert fatigue. You will also implement escalation logic where an unacknowledged alert broadens its recipient list or escalates to on-call. Dashboards and health checks give a single pane of glass for pipeline and application status. Finally, you will practice a controlled test: intentionally break a deployment action, observe CloudWatch alarms and EventBridge notifications, and then restore the change. This verifies your configuration and confirms that rollbacks, automated responses, or manual approvals behave as expected. These practices keep pipelines both observable and operable under pressure, and they embed operational discipline in your delivery process.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Notifications & Reliability
Design pattern
Granular SNS topics and escalation
Create separate topics for critical failures, approvals, and non-critical notifications. Map topics to teams and integrate via Lambda to Slack or PagerDuty for routing.
Mnemonic: Separate, Route, Escalate
Operational checks
Test alerts with controlled failures
Intentionally break a deploy, verify CloudWatch alarm fires, see EventBridge forward to SNS, and confirm team receives and acknowledges the alert. Then revert changes and document the test.
Dashboard
Single pane of glass
Build CloudWatch dashboards combining PipelineExecutionFailed counts, BuildDuration, and DeploymentSuccess metrics so you can triage quickly.
Escalation
Automatic escalation rules
Implement time-based escalation: initial alert to team channel, then escalate to on-call or PagerDuty if not acknowledged within a window.

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs — collect and query pipeline output
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Logs is the primary source of truth for debugging CI/CD failures because build and deployment output often contains the actionable error. CodeBuild automatically streams build output to CloudWatch Logs. CodeDeploy and EC2-hosted agents emit instance logs that you can forward with the CloudWatch agent, and services like ECS and Lambda write directly to logs. Use Logs Insights to query across log groups and find patterns, timestamps, or specific error messages quickly. For example, if a build fails with a dependency error, a Logs Insights query can show all similar failures across recent builds and reveal whether a transient network issue or a specific package version is the root cause. A common mistake is scanning only a single log stream; instead, query multiple streams to spot correlations between environment changes and failures. When enabling verbose tracing in buildspec or adding set -x to shell scripts, you increase signal for diagnosis but also increase log volume, so plan retention and filters. Always pair Logs Insights queries with precise time windows and sample log patterns. Key takeaway: logs give you the evidence to isolate the real problem and confirm fixes.

keyIdea.title: Logs are forensic evidence
keyIdea.text: Use CloudWatch Logs and Logs Insights to find timestamps, error patterns, and correlations across builds and deployments.

content.html:
Core Concept › CloudWatch Logs

CloudWatch Logs

Collect build and deploy output, then query with Logs Insights to surface error patterns and timestamps.

Why use Logs Insights
  • Query multiple log streams for matching error patterns or timestamps.
  • Aggregate counts of errors to detect spikes across builds.
  • Filter by log fields to speed diagnosis of environment-specific issues.
Common-mistake
Relying only on a single stream. Successful diagnosis inspects related streams and correlates timestamps with pipeline stages.
Logs Insights — sample query
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/ or @message like /AccessDenied/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 50
Concrete example
If CodeBuild shows a dependency error, query all recent build logs for that error string. A cluster of errors after a time indicates a dependency or network change.
Key Takeaway

Use Logs Insights to search, correlate, and validate fixes. Expand logging only when it helps diagnosis and retain useful indices.

screens.title: CloudWatch Metrics — measure pipeline health
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch metrics provide time-ordered measurements that reflect the state and performance of your pipeline. For CodePipeline, monitor PipelineExecutionCount, PipelineExecutionFailed, and ActionExecutionFailed to track success and failure volume. In CodeBuild, BuildDuration, FailedBuilds, and SucceededBuilds show performance and stability trends. CodeDeploy emits DeploymentSuccess, DeploymentFailure, and DeploymentDuration to surface rollout health. Use these standard metrics to populate dashboards and detect regressions before they affect users. A good dashboard combines raw counts with rates and durations, for example showing failure rate as FailedExecutions divided by ExecutionCount. Avoid alarm fatigue by setting thresholds that reflect baseline behavior; test thresholds in non-production first. Also consider anomaly detection for noisy metrics or when baseline varies. A common misconception is to create alarms for every metric. Instead, focus on metrics that affect availability or release velocity. Key takeaway: metrics give you an operational pulse; designed dashboards and thoughtful alarms turn that pulse into early warnings. CloudWatch Metrics — measure pipeline health means use standard pipeline metrics and thoughtfully designed dashboards to detect regressions and measure deployment quality.. In practical terms, key metrics to monitor for codepipeline, codebuild, and codedeploy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › CloudWatch Metrics

Key Pipeline Metrics

  • CodePipeline: PipelineExecutionCount, PipelineExecutionFailed, ActionExecutionFailed.
  • CodeBuild: BuildDuration, FailedBuilds, SucceededBuilds.
  • CodeDeploy: DeploymentSuccess, DeploymentFailure, DeploymentDuration.
Dashboard tip
Combine raw counts, rates, and rolling averages. Show recent event timeline and last failure messages to speed triage.
Metric example
Create a widget that shows BuildDuration over time and a secondary metric for FailedBuilds. A rising duration often precedes failure spikes.
Misconception
Alarming every metric causes noise. Focus alarms on user-impacting signals and use dashboards for low-priority visibility.
Key Takeaway

Select a small set of business-relevant metrics, visualize trends, and set tested alarms to catch regressions early.

screens.title: CloudWatch Alarms — trigger actions on thresholds
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Alarms watch metrics or expressions and take action when a threshold is crossed. A common pattern for CI/CD is to alarm on PipelineExecutionFailed for production pipelines and send notifications to an SNS topic subscribed by your on-call or a Lambda that triggers a rollback. When configuring an alarm, choose the right statistic and period. For example, use Sum over a five-minute period for failure counts so brief spikes don't create false positives. Alarms can publish to SNS, invoke Auto Scaling actions, or run automated remediation via Lambda. For CodeDeploy, alarms on application-specific metrics such as HTTP 5xx errors can initiate an automatic rollback using deployment hooks or automation scripts. Avoid overly aggressive thresholds that cause rollbacks for transient or external errors; instead use compound rules or anomaly detection to reduce noise. A useful test is to create a test alarm that publishes to a test SNS topic and then simulate a failure. Always include descriptive names and runbooks with your alarms so responders can act quickly and consistently. CloudWatch Alarms — trigger actions on thresholds means use well-chosen alarm thresholds and targets like sns or lambda to notify teams or trigger automated remediation without causing unnecessary churn.. In practical terms, from metric thresholds to notifications and automated rollbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › CloudWatch Alarms

Alarm lifecycle

Metric → Threshold → Action. Choose statistic and period, then attach SNS or Lambda targets for notifications or remediation.

Example alarm
Metric: PipelineExecutionFailed, Statistic: Sum, Period: 5m, Threshold: >= 1 → Action: publish to MyPipelineAlertsTopic
Pro-tip
Use composite alarms or anomaly detection to reduce noise for metrics that fluctuate often.
Key Takeaway

Design alarms with realistic thresholds and tested targets so alerts are meaningful and enable timely action.

Notification targets
  • SNS topic to email or mobile channels.
  • Lambda for custom remediation or ticket creation.
  • Auto-scaling or CodeDeploy rollback hooks for automated fixes.
Common-mistake
Tying rollbacks to noisy metrics. Test rollback triggers in staging to avoid cascading failures during transient problems.

screens.title: EventBridge — automate reactions to pipeline state changes
screens.narratorSegment: EventBridge is the glue that converts pipeline events into automated actions. You define an event pattern that matches events from CodePipeline, CodeBuild, or CodeDeploy and attach targets like SNS, Lambda, or SQS. A simple rule is to trigger a notification when a stage fails. For example, an event pattern that filters CodePipeline stage execution state changes for FAILED events will send alerts immediately. EventBridge allows you to route events to a Lambda that performs cleanup or opens a ticket, or to an SNS topic for human notification. A best practice is to make rules specific to pipeline and stage names to avoid noisy triggers. Also design the Lambda handler to be idempotent and lightweight because it may run frequently during incident storms. Testing is essential: after you create a rule, simulate a failure and verify the event arrives and the target executes as expected. Misconceptions often involve thinking EventBridge rewrites or enriches events; EventBridge routes and optionally transforms events, but your automation should include validation, retries, and error handling. EventBridge — automate reactions to pipeline state changes means use eventbridge rules to translate specific pipeline events into automated notifications or remediation steps.. In practical terms, create rules that match pipeline events and route them to targets for automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › EventBridge Rules

EventBridge rules

Match pipeline events and route them to targets like SNS or Lambda for automation or notification.

Sample event pattern
{
  "source": ["aws.codepipeline"],
  "detail-type": ["CodePipeline Stage Execution State Change"],
  "detail": {
    "state": ["FAILED"]
  }
}
Testing tip
After creating a rule, trigger a controlled failure and confirm the SNS topic or Lambda receives the event and acts correctly.
Concrete example
Create a rule that sends stage failures in ProductionWebAppPipeline to MyPipelineAlertsTopic. Add a Lambda target to format messages for Slack if desired.
Common-mistake

Make rules too broad. Narrow by pipeline and stage to avoid noisy triggers and reduce downstream load on targets.

screens.title: CloudTrail — auditing CI/CD actions and changes
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CloudTrail records A P I calls made by users, roles, and services. For pipelines this is crucial because many failures stem from permission or configuration changes. CloudTrail shows who made a call, when, from where, and what parameters were used. For example, if a CodeBuild project loses permission to push to ECR, CloudTrail can reveal a DetachRolePolicy or DeleteRolePolicy A P I call performed by a user or automation. Use CloudTrail in combination with CloudWatch Logs and the IAM Policy Simulator to determine whether a role currently has required permissions. When investigating, filter CloudTrail events for the relevant service and time window, then inspect the initiating principal. A common pitfall is ignoring CloudTrail because it feels noisy; instead, focus on narrow time slices around failure events and search for specific A P I names like PutImage or DetachRolePolicy. CloudTrail is also important for compliance and post-incident reviews because it preserves the exact sequence of actions that led to a failure. CloudTrail — auditing CI/CD actions and changes means use cloudtrail to reconstruct who made changes and when, so you can connect operational changes to pipeline failures.. In practical terms, use cloudtrail to find who changed iam, roles, or pipeline resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › CloudTrail

CloudTrail auditing

Record API activity to find who changed roles, policies, or resources that impact CI/CD pipelines.

Investigation checklist
  1. Filter CloudTrail events for the relevant time and service.
  2. Look for API calls like DetachRolePolicy, DeleteRolePolicy, or PutImage failures.
  3. Identify the principal and correlate with pipeline executions and CloudWatch logs.
Example
If ECR push fails, search CloudTrail for ecr:PutImage or authorization token calls that were denied. That shows if a role lacks the required actions or if a policy was removed.
Key Takeaway

CloudTrail is your timeline. Use it to connect configuration changes to pipeline failures and support secure post-incident reviews.

screens.title: Advanced troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Advanced troubleshooting applies a methodical checklist so you can find and fix the root cause reliably. Step one is to reproduce the issue locally when possible. For build failures, run the CodeBuild environment in Docker locally or execute build steps you see in buildspec to get faster feedback. Step two is to isolate the failing component: narrow the pipeline to the stage or action and collect the specific logs for that run. Step three uses debugging tools: enable verbose logging, add set -x to shell scripts, and check the CodeDeploy agent logs on instances. Step four is permission testing: use the IAM Policy Simulator to confirm whether a role can perform required actions. Step five is programmatic inspection with the AWS CLI: get detailed execution objects with aws codepipeline get-pipeline-execution, aws codebuild batch-get-builds, and aws codedeploy get-deployment. If you must temporarily widen permissions to restore service, always implement the permanent fix through infrastructure-as-code and revert any temporary changes afterward. This disciplined approach avoids guesswork and prevents configuration drift. Advanced troubleshooting checklist means follow a reproducible checklist: reproduce, isolate, inspect logs, simulate iam, use cli for details, and fix via iac.. In practical terms, reproduce, isolate, inspect, simulate iam, and verify fixes via iac. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Systematic diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Follow a reproducible checklist: reproduce, isolate, inspect logs, simulate IAM, use CLI for details, and fix via IaC.

content.html:
Process Flow › Troubleshooting Checklist

Checklist

  1. Reproduce the failure locally using Docker or the same environment.
  2. Isolate the pipeline stage or action causing the failure.
  3. Enable verbose logs and inspect agent/process logs.
  4. Use IAM Policy Simulator to validate permissions.
  5. Use AWS CLI calls to retrieve execution and deployment objects for context.
CLI inspection examples

screens.title: Notification strategies — granular topics vs catch-all
screens.narratorSegment: Notification design matters. Two opposing strategies are common: a single catch-all topic versus granular topics per event type or pipeline. A catch-all SNS topic is easy to set up and ensures no message is missed, but it leads to noise and alert fatigue. Granular topics let you route messages based on severity and event type. For example, severe production pipeline failures go to a PagerDuty or critical channel, while development pipeline failures go to a team channel. Use Lambda functions as targets when you need to enrich or conditionally route messages to third-party integrations like Slack. Also implement escalation: initial notifications go to a primary channel, and if unacknowledged, the alert expands to on-call or management channels. Dashboards and health checks supplement notifications by providing situational awareness without raising immediate alerts for low-impact metrics. A balanced approach is to use granular topics for critical signals and a broader dashboard for trends. Always document runbooks linked to each notification so responders know the expected steps. Notification strategies — granular topics vs catch-all means prefer granular topics for critical paths and reserve broad channels for informational events to reduce noise and speed response.. In practical terms, how to route alerts to avoid fatigue and ensure critical issues reach the right people. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Catch-all channel
Pros: simple to configure and guarantees delivery. Cons: high noise, harder to prioritize and escalate critical incidents.

screens.title: Assessment: Diagnose an ECR push Access Denied
screens.narratorSegment: You receive an Access Denied error when CodeBuild tries to push an image to Amazon ECR. Start by examining CloudWatch Logs for the exact error string and the repository name. Next, inspect the CodeBuild project's service role because missing ECR permissions are the most common cause. Use CloudTrail to search for ecr:PutImage and related A P I calls that failed around the failure time to identify who or what initiated the change. Use the IAM Policy Simulator to validate the role's permissions against required ECR actions. If the role lacks actions like ecr:PutImage, ecr:InitiateLayerUpload, ecr:UploadLayerPart, and ecr:CompleteLayerUpload, update the role's policy. Implement the change through your IaC templates so the fix is version-controlled. After updating, run a build to confirm the push now succeeds. Be cautious about temporary broad permission grants in production; if you must unblock the pipeline rapidly, revert broad changes and apply a minimal permanent policy through IaC. This process ensures you fix the root cause and prevent future drift. Assessment: Diagnose an ECR push Access Denied means confirm the error in logs, trace failing api calls in cloudtrail, validate via iam simulator, and fix permissions via infrastructure-as-code.. In practical terms, stepwise diagnosis and permanent resolution for a codebuild push failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Assessment: EventBridge rules for Slack and PagerDuty
screens.narratorSegment: To meet the requirement of notifying Slack on any action failure and PagerDuty on full pipeline failures, create two EventBridge rules. First rule: match CodePipeline Action Execution State Change with state FAILED and pipeline name ProductionWebAppPipeline. Set a Lambda target that formats and posts to Slack, or send to an SNS topic wired to a Slack integration. Second rule: match CodePipeline Pipeline Execution State Change with state FAILED for the same pipeline. Send that event to a different Lambda or SNS topic that integrates with PagerDuty. Use separate targets so the channels and escalation policies differ. Test both rules by simulating an action failure and a full pipeline failure to ensure each target receives the expected event shape. Ensure the Lambdas are idempotent and include retry/error handling because third-party endpoints can be rate-limited. This separation provides granular alerts for action-level problems and critical alerts for full execution failures, matching operational needs and escalation paths. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to make CI/CD pipelines reliable by adding deep observability, event-driven automation, and audit trails. We start with CloudWatch logs and metrics so you can see what's happening in builds, tests, and deployments. Then we use EventBridge to react to failures automatically, and CloudTrail to trace who or what changed permissions or resources. You will also learn systematic troubleshooting steps: reproduce failures locally, isolate the failing action, use verbose logging and the IAM policy simulator, and use AWS CLI methods to inspect executions. Finally, we cover notification design and escalation so incidents reach the right people quickly. These practices reduce mean time to detection and recovery, and help prevent recurring outages. For example, you will configure an alarm on PipelineExecutionFailed and an EventBridge rule that sends an SNS notice, then test by intentionally breaking a deployment. That hands-on workflow ties monitoring, automation, and auditing into a repeatable operational pattern.

By the end of these screens you will be able to define and implement comprehensive monitoring for CodePipeline, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy using CloudWatch. You will configure EventBridge rules that trigger automated actions when pipeline state changes occur, such as sending notifications or invoking diagnostic Lambdas. You will also use CloudTrail logs to audit pipeline activity and identify who or what changed a resource. Each objective ties a specific capability to why it matters: alarms reduce detection time, EventBridge enables automated responses, and CloudTrail provides forensic context for security and compliance. For example, creating a CloudWatch alarm on PipelineExecutionFailed and wiring it to an SNS topic gives immediate operational visibility. These skills let you build pipelines that are not only functional but observable, automatable, and auditable. You will practice these steps in a hands-on activity that walks through alarm creation, rule definition, and test failure scenarios so you can verify competency in real environments.

This second objective screen focuses on notifications, escalation policies, and testable practices. You will learn to design granular notification topics for different event types so messages reach the correct teams. For example, separate SNS topics for critical production failures and for development pipeline noise prevent alert fatigue. You will also implement escalation logic where an unacknowledged alert broadens its recipient list or escalates to on-call. Dashboards and health checks give a single pane of glass for pipeline and application status. Finally, you will practice a controlled test: intentionally break a deployment action, observe CloudWatch alarms and EventBridge notifications, and then restore the change. This verifies your configuration and confirms that rollbacks, automated responses, or manual approvals behave as expected. These practices keep pipelines both observable and operable under pressure, and they embed operational discipline in your delivery process.

CloudWatch Logs is the primary source of truth for debugging CI/CD failures because build and deployment output often contains the actionable error. CodeBuild automatically streams build output to CloudWatch Logs. CodeDeploy and EC2-hosted agents emit instance logs that you can forward with the CloudWatch agent, and services like ECS and Lambda write directly to logs. Use Logs Insights to query across log groups and find patterns, timestamps, or specific error messages quickly. For example, if a build fails with a dependency error, a Logs Insights query can show all similar failures across recent builds and reveal whether a transient network issue or a specific package version is the root cause. A common mistake is scanning only a single log stream; instead, query multiple streams to spot correlations between environment changes and failures. When enabling verbose tracing in buildspec or adding set -x to shell scripts, you increase signal for diagnosis but also increase log volume, so plan retention and filters. Always pair Logs Insights queries with precise time windows and sample log patterns. Key takeaway: logs give you the evidence to isolate the real problem and confirm fixes.

CloudWatch metrics provide time-ordered measurements that reflect the state and performance of your pipeline. For CodePipeline, monitor PipelineExecutionCount, PipelineExecutionFailed, and ActionExecutionFailed to track success and failure volume. In CodeBuild, BuildDuration, FailedBuilds, and SucceededBuilds show performance and stability trends. CodeDeploy emits DeploymentSuccess, DeploymentFailure, and DeploymentDuration to surface rollout health. Use these standard metrics to populate dashboards and detect regressions before they affect users. A good dashboard combines raw counts with rates and durations, for example showing failure rate as FailedExecutions divided by ExecutionCount. Avoid alarm fatigue by setting thresholds that reflect baseline behavior; test thresholds in non-production first. Also consider anomaly detection for noisy metrics or when baseline varies. A common misconception is to create alarms for every metric. Instead, focus on metrics that affect availability or release velocity. Key takeaway: metrics give you an operational pulse; designed dashboards and thoughtful alarms turn that pulse into early warnings. CloudWatch Metrics — measure pipeline health means use standard pipeline metrics and thoughtfully designed dashboards to detect regressions and measure deployment quality.. In practical terms, key metrics to monitor for codepipeline, codebuild, and codedeploy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CloudWatch Alarms watch metrics or expressions and take action when a threshold is crossed. A common pattern for CI/CD is to alarm on PipelineExecutionFailed for production pipelines and send notifications to an SNS topic subscribed by your on-call or a Lambda that triggers a rollback. When configuring an alarm, choose the right statistic and period. For example, use Sum over a five-minute period for failure counts so brief spikes don't create false positives. Alarms can publish to SNS, invoke Auto Scaling actions, or run automated remediation via Lambda. For CodeDeploy, alarms on application-specific metrics such as HTTP 5xx errors can initiate an automatic rollback using deployment hooks or automation scripts. Avoid overly aggressive thresholds that cause rollbacks for transient or external errors; instead use compound rules or anomaly detection to reduce noise. A useful test is to create a test alarm that publishes to a test SNS topic and then simulate a failure. Always include descriptive names and runbooks with your alarms so responders can act quickly and consistently. CloudWatch Alarms — trigger actions on thresholds means use well-chosen alarm thresholds and targets like sns or lambda to notify teams or trigger automated remediation without causing unnecessary churn.. In practical terms, from metric thresholds to notifications and automated rollbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EventBridge is the glue that converts pipeline events into automated actions. You define an event pattern that matches events from CodePipeline, CodeBuild, or CodeDeploy and attach targets like SNS, Lambda, or SQS. A simple rule is to trigger a notification when a stage fails. For example, an event pattern that filters CodePipeline stage execution state changes for FAILED events will send alerts immediately. EventBridge allows you to route events to a Lambda that performs cleanup or opens a ticket, or to an SNS topic for human notification. A best practice is to make rules specific to pipeline and stage names to avoid noisy triggers. Also design the Lambda handler to be idempotent and lightweight because it may run frequently during incident storms. Testing is essential: after you create a rule, simulate a failure and verify the event arrives and the target executes as expected. Misconceptions often involve thinking EventBridge rewrites or enriches events; EventBridge routes and optionally transforms events, but your automation should include validation, retries, and error handling. EventBridge — automate reactions to pipeline state changes means use eventbridge rules to translate specific pipeline events into automated notifications or remediation steps.. In practical terms, create rules that match pipeline events and route them to targets for automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS CloudTrail records A P I calls made by users, roles, and services. For pipelines this is crucial because many failures stem from permission or configuration changes. CloudTrail shows who made a call, when, from where, and what parameters were used. For example, if a CodeBuild project loses permission to push to ECR, CloudTrail can reveal a DetachRolePolicy or DeleteRolePolicy A P I call performed by a user or automation. Use CloudTrail in combination with CloudWatch Logs and the IAM Policy Simulator to determine whether a role currently has required permissions. When investigating, filter CloudTrail events for the relevant service and time window, then inspect the initiating principal. A common pitfall is ignoring CloudTrail because it feels noisy; instead, focus on narrow time slices around failure events and search for specific A P I names like PutImage or DetachRolePolicy. CloudTrail is also important for compliance and post-incident reviews because it preserves the exact sequence of actions that led to a failure. CloudTrail — auditing CI/CD actions and changes means use cloudtrail to reconstruct who made changes and when, so you can connect operational changes to pipeline failures.. In practical terms, use cloudtrail to find who changed iam, roles, or pipeline resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Advanced troubleshooting applies a methodical checklist so you can find and fix the root cause reliably. Step one is to reproduce the issue locally when possible. For build failures, run the CodeBuild environment in Docker locally or execute build steps you see in buildspec to get faster feedback. Step two is to isolate the failing component: narrow the pipeline to the stage or action and collect the specific logs for that run. Step three uses debugging tools: enable verbose logging, add set -x to shell scripts, and check the CodeDeploy agent logs on instances. Step four is permission testing: use the IAM Policy Simulator to confirm whether a role can perform required actions. Step five is programmatic inspection with the AWS CLI: get detailed execution objects with aws codepipeline get-pipeline-execution, aws codebuild batch-get-builds, and aws codedeploy get-deployment. Notification design matters. Two opposing strategies are common: a single catch-all topic versus granular topics per event type or pipeline. A catch-all SNS topic is easy to set up and ensures no message is missed, but it leads to noise and alert fatigue. Granular topics let you route messages based on severity and event type. For example, severe production pipeline failures go to a PagerDuty or critical channel, while development pipeline failures go to a team channel. Use Lambda functions as targets when you need to enrich or conditionally route messages to third-party integrations like Slack. Also implement escalation: initial notifications go to a primary channel, and if unacknowledged, the alert expands to on-call or management channels. Dashboards and health checks supplement notifications by providing situational awareness without raising immediate alerts for low-impact metrics. A balanced approach is to use granular topics for critical signals and a broader dashboard for trends. Always document runbooks linked to each notification so responders know the expected steps. If the role lacks actions like ecr:PutImage, ecr:InitiateLayerUpload, ecr:UploadLayerPart, and ecr:CompleteLayerUpload, update the role's policy.
